1.pericope_label: The persecution after Stephen, his burial, and Saul's havoc

schools.summary: Gill places the opening clause at the end of the preceding chapter on the authority of the versions and the Alexandrian copy, reads the verb as consent with pleasure, explains that the record of Saul's part is given because the persecutor became a preacher, and recalls the prophecy that Benjamin should ravin as a wolf; Calvin compares the wicked to beasts that thirst for blood once they have tasted it, warns that a martyr must not be blamed for whetting his enemies' cruelty, applies the lull in persecution to his own age, denies that the whole Church fled and explains the flight as necessity rather than panic, makes standing against wolves the pastor's duty, sees the middle wall falling as the fugitives reach Samaria, and defends the burial as belonging to the hope of the resurrection.

Henry supposes Paul had the notice of his own consent inserted for shame to himself and glory to free grace, observes that Stephen's dying prayers only exasperated his enemies further, distinguishes the scattered preachers from the whole body of believers, reads the dispersal as an intimation of Providence sending them to work elsewhere, takes the devout men either for proselytes or for the more zealous of the church, and gives three reasons for the burial, ending with the testimony it bore to the resurrection.

Clarke glosses the verb as gladly consenting, traces the persecution to the Jews' inability to bear the doctrine of the resurrection, insists the disciples fled in obedience and not from fear, reports Bishop Pearce's doubts of Eusebius on the apostles' early travels and denies Rome's precedence to the first church at Jerusalem, quotes a father's image of the fugitives as lamps lit at the Spirit's fire, argues from the public lamentation that Stephen was never condemned by the Sanhedrin, and explains the executions Paul owned by Roman authority or by the mob's judgment of zeal; Wesley denies that the whole Church was scattered and calls Saul a furious beast of prey.

Ellicott finds the word for consenting carefully chosen to show that Saul directed rather than threw, argues from Paul's later usage that he judged his own guilt the greater, explains the choice of Samaria and finds the old antipathy already breaking down, gives two reasons for the apostles' staying including the twelve-year tradition in Clement and Eusebius, refutes Renan's claim that the mourners were proselytes on lexical grounds, and reports Augustine's tradition about Gamaliel and Nicodemus; Barnes calls this the first of a series of persecutions and finds good brought out of evil; Robertson parses the participle, notes that Sadducees and Pharisees were now united, and leaves the sparing of the apostles an open puzzle; Lightfoot supplies the rabbinic rule forbidding lamentation over one the Sanhedrin condemned.

debates: Who the devout men were: Jews who were not Christians, as Barnes and Ellicott hold and Robertson allows; proselytes, as Renan argued and Ellicott refutes; or members of the church, as Henry and Calvin assume
Why the apostles alone remained: pastoral duty, obedience to the command to begin at Jerusalem, a twelve-year tradition, their popularity, or Gamaliel's earlier advice — Robertson leaves it undecided
Whether Stephen was condemned by the Sanhedrin at all, which Clarke denies on the ground that the public lamentation was forbidden in such cases
outliers: Clarke turns aside to deny the precedence of the Church of Rome on the ground that Jerusalem was the first Christian church, and to record the burial customs by which the instruments of execution were interred with the condemned
Ellicott records the later translation of Stephen's relics to Ancona, Minorca and Africa, and the legend that his name appeared on the tomb in Aramaic as Chaliel, a garland

4.pericope_label: The scattered preach, and Philip in Samaria

schools.summary: Gill treats the unclean spirits and the cures as specimens of a larger work; Calvin sees providence bringing light out of darkness so that the gospel once heard in one place sounds everywhere, warns that the first exercises of martyrdom must not make us dumb, identifies the city as the one Hyrcanus laid waste and Herod rebuilt as Sebaste, sums the gospel in Christ who reconciles and regenerates, and traces the order of hearing, miracle and attentiveness as the right approach to faith.

Henry reads the scattering through Samson's riddle and finds the persecution overruled to enlarge the church, notes that the preachers now entered the Samaritan cities once forbidden them, allows either Sebaste or Sychem for the city, observes that Christ sent his gospel to slay the enmity between Jew and Samaritan, describes the preaching as the proclamation of a king at his accession, calls the miracles the broad seal of heaven annexed to the commission, and reads the loud cry of the spirits as the mark of a reluctant departure.

Clarke denies that any city called Samaria then existed, cites Josephus on its destruction by Hyrcanus and rebuilding by Herod, adds Bishop Pearce's argument from Luke's consistent naming of Caesarea and prefers Shechem with Gerizim as the seat of Samaritan religion, explains why the Samaritans as a link between Jew and Gentile were evangelised first, and argues that the unclean spirits cannot be a species of disease since they are distinguished from the palsied and the lame; Wesley notes that the narrative is resumed verbatim in the eleventh chapter.

Ellicott takes the fugitives for Stephen's Hellenistic fellow-workers, renders the phrase a city and identifies it with Sychar, explains Philip's choice by the earlier sowing there, notes that the identity of name misled Polycrates as quoted by Eusebius, prefers signs to miracles and argues that they strengthened rather than founded the Samaritans' faith, and suggests Luke had the account from Philip at Caesarea; Barnes denies that a city of Samaria existed and refuses the inference that deacons are an order with a right to preach; Robertson makes Samaria the city's own name, distinguishes the verbs for evangelising and heralding, and notes an anacoluthon in the best text; Lightfoot weighs Sebaste against Sychem and observes that the later report suits a city rather than a province.

debates: Which city Philip preached in: the rebuilt capital Sebaste, as Robertson's grammar and Henry's first reading suggest, or Shechem and Sychar, as Clarke with Pearce and Ellicott prefer, Lightfoot leaving the question open
Whether the unclean spirits are a class of disease, which Clarke denies on the ground that the text distinguishes them from the palsied and the lame
Whether Philip's preaching establishes a right of deacons to preach, which Barnes denies
outliers: Barnes turns aside from the narrative to argue a point of church order, that nothing here makes deacons an order of ministers under the New Testament economy
Ellicott and Robertson independently suggest that Luke's information for this chapter came from Philip himself during the stay at Caesarea

9.pericope_label: Simon the sorcerer, and the baptism of the Samaritans

schools.summary: Gill passes briefly over the sorcery and notes that Simon kept close to Philip; Calvin reads the title Great as designed to make all else divine grow vile, praises Philip for setting his hand to the work though he saw no way through, treats the bewitching of a city as the common punishment of unbelief, refuses the opinion that Simon merely feigned since Luke says he believed, proposes a mean between faith and dissimulation in men overcome by the Word who think they believe, and explains that God meant to triumph over a reputed demigod by making him own the true miracles.

Clarke reports the ecclesiastical legends about Simon and dismisses them as extravagancies, derives sorcerer from the Latin for casting lots and magic from the Persian priesthood, prefers the fuller reading of the title with a list of authorities while confessing he cannot say what the Samaritans meant by it, takes Simon's faith at face value as conviction produced by real miracles, and argues from the identity of the verbs that bewitched is an improper rendering in the earlier verses; Wesley notes only that magic was then a real thing and that it was Philip's preaching they believed.

Ellicott makes Simon the type of a class of Jewish pretenders and holds the legends about him not incredible, explains the title from the Samaritan use of powers for the angels of God, traces the people's credulity to the impression the Saviour had left among them, and calls Simon's faith a formless faith neither preceded by repentance nor perfected by love; Barnes denies outright that he was a real Christian, explains his profession by the pressure of the multitude, and observes that Philip could not know the heart; Robertson reviews and rejects the traditions, including Baur's identification with Paul and Justin Martyr's Roman statue, which an inscription found in the Tiber shows to name a Sabine Hercules; Lightfoot notes Simon's continuance with Philip.

Cyril of Jerusalem takes the baptisms as occasion for the doctrine itself, that man being of a twofold nature the purification is twofold, water cleansing the body while the Spirit seals the soul, and that neither the baptized who lack the Spirit nor the virtuous who lack the seal of water receive the grace in perfection.

debates: Whether Simon truly believed: Barnes denies it outright and Ellicott calls the faith formless, while Calvin expressly refuses the charge of feigning and posits a temporary faith between belief and dissimulation, and Clarke takes the profession at face value

What weight the later legends about Simon carry: Clarke calls them extravagancies that never existed, Ellicott thinks them not incredible, and Robertson refutes the Roman statue from an inscription found in the Tiber
Whether bewitched is a proper rendering, which Clarke denies on the ground that the same verb describes Simon's own amazement at Philip
outliers: Robertson records that the stone recovered from the Tiber in 1574, long cited as evidence for Justin Martyr's account of Simon worshipped at Rome, is inscribed to a Sabine name for Hercules

14.pericope_label: Peter and John sent to Samaria, and the gift of the Holy Ghost

schools.summary: Gill describes the laying on of hands plainly; Calvin states at length the difficulty that baptism must be empty if it can be separated from the Spirit, answers that Luke means not the common grace of regeneration but the singular gifts given at the beginning to beautify Christ's kingdom, holds that the Samaritans already had the Spirit of adoption, denies that anything here disparages baptism, and argues from the order of prayer before the laying on of hands that the grace is not shut up in the ceremony though the effect is annexed to it.

Henry explains the mission by the limits of an evangelist's office and the powers reserved to apostles, observes that Peter submitted to an order of the house rather than sending others, adds that ministers in a higher station should help those in a lower, identifies what was lacking as the extraordinary Pentecostal powers and especially tongues, and draws the pastoral consequence that the sanctified have no reason to complain for want of gifts that would only make them bright.

Clarke explains the idiom of going down from Jerusalem as the usage proper to any imperial city and warns against inferring anything about its elevation, argues that the gift conferred cannot have been sanctification, which believers already had and no apostle dispensed, but the miraculous gifts needed for public work, and insists that a deacon full of the Spirit could not confer it while the apostles themselves were only instruments through whom the blessing came from God; he also holds with Barnes that the hands were not laid on all.

Ellicott reads the mission as the formal end of the limit that had excluded Samaria, notes the irony that the apostle who once sought fire on a Samaritan village now brought the baptism of the Spirit, takes the phrase of outward and visible gifts, and traces the laying on of hands forward as the starting-point of Confirmation while admitting the question whether it was normal or exceptional and dating the modern explanation of the name no further back than the sixteenth century; Barnes and Robertson note the unusual expression that the Spirit had fallen on none of them, and Barnes with Clarke restricts the imposition of hands to a few prominent persons, since it was plainly not laid on Simon; Lightfoot and Robertson report the sending itself.

Cyril of Jerusalem turns the promise of the Comforter against Manes, who claimed that title for himself although the promise had been fulfilled to the apostles who were told to tarry in Jerusalem until they were endued with power from on high.

debates: What the Samaritans lacked when they had been baptized but had not received the Spirit: Calvin says the singular gifts and not the common grace of regeneration, which they already had; Clarke says the miraculous gifts needed for public work and not sanctification; Henry says the Pentecostal powers and especially tongues
Whether the laying on of hands here is the origin of a standing rite: Ellicott traces Confirmation to it while admitting the practice may have been exceptional
On how many hands were laid, Barnes and Clarke both arguing from Simon's exclusion that it was only a few
outliers: Ellicott dates the explanation of Confirmation as adults confirming their baptismal promises no earlier than the sixteenth century, against its common assumption

18.pericope_label: Simon offers money, and Peter's answer

schools.summary: Gill notes the abhorrence with which Peter answered; Calvin argues that Simon's earlier profession was not feigned but unregenerate, calls the case a mixing of Christ with Satan where doctrine never reaches the hidden affections, enumerates four distinct offences in the offer, and holds that Peter's curse was the sentence of a judge on what the offence deserved rather than a wish for destruction, since he would rather have had Simon saved.

Clarke reads the curse conditionally, as importing that unless he repented he and his goods would perish together, and observes that Peter informs not Simon only but all who come after that the Spirit is God's gift and cannot be bought, since the silver and gold are already his; Wesley names the sin simony after this offer, distinguishes part from lot as purchase from free gift, and argues from Paul's leaving Trophimus sick and nearly losing Epaphroditus that no apostle had a universal power of discerning hearts.

Ellicott renders the curse literally as money going with its owner to perdition, notes the recurrence of the same word and of the gold that perishes in the epistles ascribed to Peter as bearing on their authorship, observes that Peter uses the very word for free receiving that the Lord had spoken to the Twelve, and takes part and lot of an inheritance in the Church's gifts and offices; Barnes reads the curse conditionally and explains the two words alike; Robertson parses the optative as a wish revealing Peter's indignation and holds that the natural sense puts Simon on the road to destruction though repentance remained open; Lightfoot argues that the apostles could impart the gifts but not the power of imparting them, which was purely apostolical and died with them.

Cyril of Jerusalem fastens on the exact terms of the request, that Simon asked not for the fellowship of the Holy Ghost but for the power, meaning to sell what cannot be sold and what he did not possess, and calls him a second Judas for offering money to men who had just trodden underfoot the prices laid at their feet.

debates: How far Peter's words are a curse: Calvin makes them a judicial sentence on the offence rather than a wish, Robertson an indignant optative putting Simon on the road to destruction, and Clarke and Barnes a conditional warning that assumes impenitence
Whether an apostle could discern any man's heart at will, which Wesley denies from Paul's inability to heal at will
outliers: Lightfoot observes that no apostle could confer the power of conferring the gifts, so that Simon's request was for something even the apostles could not grant
Ellicott turns a verbal coincidence in this verse into evidence bearing on the authorship of the Second Epistle of Peter

22.pericope_label: Peter's call to repentance, Simon's answer, and the return to Jerusalem

schools.summary: Gill takes Peter's perception as a judgement drawn from the act rather than a revelation, and notes the preaching on the way back; Calvin reads the call to repentance as proof that Peter sought Simon's recovery, observes that he reproves him sharply a second time, and infers from the request for others' prayers that Simon did not take the rebuke as he ought.

Clarke explains the gall of bitterness as a Hebraism and compares the roots of gall and wormwood in Deuteronomy and Hebrews, sees in the bond of iniquity the Roman practice of chaining a prisoner to his guard, alone hopes well of Simon's repentance on the strength of the reading in the Codex Bezae and the later Syriac margin that he wept greatly and did not cease, and dismisses the legends of the flight before Claudius and the rest as utterly unworthy of credit; Wesley notes the conditional form of the exhortation.

Ellicott insists the stern words were meant to heal and not to slay, weighs whether Peter feared the sin against the Holy Ghost and finds it suggestive that he neither forgives nor condemns but leaves judgment to the Judge, notes the only figurative use of gall in the New Testament and takes the bond of iniquity for an inveterate habit, reads Simon's reply as fear of penalty rather than of sin and as recourse to a human mediator, sets out the later legends in full including the Roman inscription reported by Justin, and follows Samaria forward to the destruction of Sychem and the founding of Flavia Neapolis; Barnes draws the rule that sinners ask others to pray while too much in love with sin to pray themselves and concludes that Simon died impenitent; Robertson traces the word for gall and marks the resumption of the narrative.
Cyril of Jerusalem closes the episode with the exhortation to rejoice in the Lord.

debates: Whether Simon repented: Clarke hopes well of him on the strength of a Western reading that he wept and did not cease, while Barnes and Ellicott both read the reply as fear of punishment rather than sorrow for sin and take the testimony of antiquity as decisive against him

What weight the Simon legends carry: Ellicott reports them at length, including the Roman altar inscribed to Simon as a holy god which Robertson elsewhere shows to name a Sabine deity, while Clarke pronounces the whole utterly unworthy of credit
outliers: Clarke rests his one hopeful reading of Simon's fate on the Codex Bezae and the margin of the later Syriac, which add that he wept greatly and did not cease
Ellicott finds it terribly suggestive that Peter, holding the power of the keys, here neither forgives nor condemns but stands midway between hope and fear

26.pericope_label: The angel sends Philip southward, and the Ethiopian in his chariot

schools.summary: Gill notes that the eunuch was returning from worship; Calvin draws from Philip's obedience the rule that whoever commits the success to God finds all fall out well that is undertaken at his appointment, holds that eastern courtiers were called eunuchs promiscuously though they were men, explains Candace as a name of office borne by all the queens as Caesar was by the emperors, and finds in the reading itself a mind still seeking to profit.

Henry observes that Philip stayed behind to break fresh ground, that he was sent to a common road through a wilderness where there was small likelihood of work, that God sometimes opens a door in unlikely places, and that Philip went without asking what business he had there; he heads the story with the psalm of Ethiopia stretching out her hands and distinguishes this Ethiopia from the Arabian.

Clarke holds that eunuch was a court title not requiring the literal sense, instancing the married Potiphar, and derives the name Gaza from a Persian word for riches on Servius's authority that Cambyses stored his treasure there, tracing the word through Arabic to the modern magazine; Wesley states the two roads from Jerusalem plainly and agrees that chief officers were anciently so called.

Ellicott would read an angel rather than the angel, notes that the tenses set these events alongside the journey of Peter and John, leaves open whether the clause about the desert is the angel's or Luke's while inclining to the southern route through Hebron, traces the history of Gaza from the Canaanites to the Maccabees, explains the long working of Jewish influence in Ethiopia from Manasseh onward, and argues from the usage of the Gospels for the strict sense of eunuch, connecting the man's admission with Isaiah's relaxation of the law of Deuteronomy and with the rule framed at Nicaea; Lightfoot assigns the clause to the angel and explains it as distinguishing the Philistine Gaza from the Gaza of Ephraim; Robertson glosses the direction and the office; Barnes describes the treasury charge and the carriage.

Chrysostom argues from the southward direction that this Philip must be one of the Seven, since from Jerusalem the road would run north, notes that a desert road meant no fear of Jewish attack, presses Philip's asking no reason but going, and praises the eunuch for coming from Ethiopia to worship when no festival was held and for studying as he rode.

debates: Whether the eunuch was one in the literal sense, which Ellicott maintains from the usage of the Gospels while Clarke, Calvin and Wesley take the word for a court title only

Who says that the way is desert and what is meant: Lightfoot assigns it to the angel and makes it distinguish two cities named Gaza, while Ellicott leaves the speaker open and refers it rather to the less frequented southern road
outliers: Clarke turns aside to derive the name Gaza from Persian, tracing it through Arabic and Spanish to the English word magazine
Chrysostom infers the identity of this Philip from the compass direction of the road he is sent along

29.pericope_label: Philip joins the chariot, and the passage of Isaiah

schools.summary: Gill notes the change from an angel's word to the Spirit's and the passage read; Calvin praises the eunuch's modesty in letting a common man question him and confessing his ignorance, turns it against a generation in which scarcely one man in a hundred submits himself to learn, insists that to own a wisdom in Scripture surpassing us is the true reverence for it, allows either that the eunuch had the Greek volume or that Luke gave the version then in use, and reads the prophecy of a Christ exalted out of sorrow and judgment who comes up from the depth of death as conqueror.

Clarke takes the Spirit's speaking for a mark that this direction was internal where the former was by an angel, and on the great crux reports the Jewish custom of calling out at an execution whether any could speak to the criminal's manner of life, a benevolent inquiry never made in our Lord's case, and prefers that sense while recording the readings which refer the words to the eternal Sonship, the miraculous conception or the spiritual progeny; Wesley describes Philip's running and notes the portion read.

Barnes shows from the variation that the eunuch was reading the Greek version, explains that the Hebrew word for prison covers any detention or oppression so that humiliation is not far from it, takes the sense to be that justice was denied him in his lowest estate, and reports Lowth's rendering of the disputed noun as manner of life; Ellicott sets out the competing constructions of both the Hebrew and the Greek and lists three senses of the harder question, preferring that which makes it the wickedness of the generation; Robertson glosses the verb for joining, the condition in the eunuch's reply and the tense of the disputed verb; Lightfoot argues from another passage that the word rendered prison means detention on a religious account, so that Christ was snatched from his devotion as well as from justice, and reads the question of the generation as the wickedness of the age.
Cyril of Jerusalem cites the Spirit's direction of Philip as evidence that the Spirit chooses and appoints rather than being a mere impersonal power.

debates: What in his humiliation his judgment was taken away means: Barnes takes it of justice denied him at his lowest estate, Ellicott sets out four constructions of the Hebrew and Greek together, Calvin makes it his exaltation out of sorrow and judgment, and Lightfoot has him snatched from the place of his devotion as well as from judgment

What who shall declare his generation means: Clarke prefers the failure of the customary inquiry into a condemned man's life, Lightfoot and Ellicott the wickedness of the age, Barnes reports Lowth's manner of life, and Clarke records readings that refer it to the eternal Sonship or the miraculous conception
outliers: Calvin turns the eunuch's confession of ignorance into a rebuke of his own age, where men would rather nourish their ignorance than be seen as another man's scholar

34.pericope_label: The eunuch's question, Philip's preaching, and the baptism

schools.summary: Gill describes the freedom and boldness of Philip's discourse and expounds the confession as it stands; Calvin finds in the question the proof of an earnest desire to learn, explains the opening of the mouth as Scripture's mark of a weighty discourse, grants that the men of old put the whole body into the water where the use now is to sprinkle, and refuses to divide the Church over so small a difference of ceremony while holding that for baptism itself we ought to fight a hundred times to death.

Clarke explains why the doubt was natural, the prophecy standing as of a man already dead, presses the force of beginning at the same scripture rather than leaving it for another, remarks that the eunuch was unwilling to lose the opportunity, and supposes he plunged himself as the Jews commonly did while the baptism was still attributed to the man who received his confession; Wesley notes the going down out of the chariot.

Ellicott reports that Jewish teachers had referred the passage to the nation or to Jeremiah, so that the doubt was real, calls the confession a striking illustration of the early tendency to improve the text for edification, notes that Irenaeus quotes it though the best manuscripts including the Sinaitic omit it, explains the motive of the interpolation, finds the confession's shortness a mark of very early liturgy, and defends immersion from the universal practice of the early Church, picturing the whole action and quoting the Fathers on the Ethiopian changing his skin; Barnes reports the same textual doubt and its rejection by the ablest critics while keeping the substance, takes the terms of the confession for the standing qualification of a profession, and answers the argument from the preposition with a string of parallels while denying that entering the water proves immersion; Robertson gives the bare force of the words and the participle of beginning.
Cyril of Jerusalem argues from the same principle that lies behind the confession, that no man can say Jesus Christ is Lord but by the Holy Ghost, and applies it to the witness of the martyrs.

debates: Whether the baptism was by immersion: Ellicott defends it from the universal practice of the early Church, Barnes denies that either the preposition or the entering into the water proves it, Clarke supposes a self-plunging after the Jewish manner, and Calvin grants the ancient practice while defending the modern
Whether the eunuch's confession of faith belongs to the text: Barnes and Ellicott both judge it an early insertion, though Barnes keeps its doctrine and Gill and Clarke expound it as it stands
outliers: Calvin will not divide the Church over the mode of baptism yet says we should fight a hundred times to death rather than let the ceremony itself be taken away
Ellicott records the Fathers' half-playful application of the prophet's question about the Ethiopian's skin to this convert

39.pericope_label: The Spirit takes Philip away, and the preaching from Azotus to Caesarea

schools.summary: Gill notes the departure and the eunuch's joy; Calvin observes that Luke concludes the history by showing nothing was lacking to the eunuch's instruction, makes the rejoicing proof that he lost nothing by losing his teacher, and cites Josephus on the city of Caesarea.

Clarke holds that the catching away means no more than a suggestion of the Spirit that Philip should withdraw abruptly, rejects the notion of a bodily transport like Habakkuk's in the Apocrypha, reports the Alexandrian variant, identifies Azotus with the Old Testament Ashdod and cites Herodotus on the twenty-nine years' siege by Psammetichus, infers that Philip must have preached through the Philistine cities and Samaria on his way, distinguishes Caesarea from Caesarea Philippi, and closes on Philip's household and prophesying daughters and the duty of bringing up a family that no man can discharge by substitute; Wesley states the disappearance in a line.

Barnes continues his argument from the prepositions, holding that out of the water proves no more than into it did, and traces the route; Ellicott takes the catching away literally as an irresistible impulse that snatched Philip from his companion, compares the Spirit's hindering of Paul, reports and weighs the more material reading with its parallels in Elijah, Ezekiel and Paul, settles on a suspension of ordinary consciousness illustrated by Bernard beside the Lake of Geneva, and judges the Alexandrian variant a conjectural emendation; Lightfoot computes the distance from Gaza to Azotus; Robertson marks the imperfect that makes the preaching continuous through every city.
Cyril of Jerusalem returns to the Spirit's personal action in directing Philip throughout the episode.

debates: What the catching away of Philip was: Clarke makes it only an inward suggestion to withdraw and denies any need of a bodily transport, while Ellicott takes it as a literal snatching away in a state of ecstasy and reports that many have understood a body caught up into the air
Whether the Alexandrian reading, that the Spirit fell on the eunuch and an angel caught away Philip, has any claim on the text, which Ellicott denies
outliers: Clarke ends the chapter on a domestic duty, that a man's bringing up of his family in the knowledge of God can be discharged by no substitute and cannot be neglected without endangering his own salvation
